newsitem.title: USA: U.S. senators say they could pass chemical treaty.
newsitem.headline: U.S. senators say they could pass chemical treaty.

text.p: Key U.S. senators said on Thursday there were enough votes in the Senate to approve a global treaty outlawing chemical weapons but it was unclear how it will be pried from the grip of Sen. Jesse Helms.
Helms, a North Carolina Republican and leading Senate foe of the Chemical Weapons Convention, has the treaty before the Foreign Relations Committee, of which he is chairman.

He has given no indication when, or if, he will allow the committee to vote to send it to the full Senate -- even though Republican Leader Trent Lott has promised to bring it to a Senate vote this month.

With time running out on an April 29 deadline when the treaty takes effect, with or without the United States, Helms was raising the prospect of additional hearings next week following up testimony over the past two days.

Sen Joseph Biden of Delaware, the committee's top Democrat, said on Thursday he still hoped Helms would allow the treaty out of his grip. But he said if Helms remained adamant there were other ways to get it to the full Senate -- a committee discharge vote and action by Lott.
"The simple proposition is: Sen Lott is going to have to pull the trigger, so to speak," Biden said.
"I cannot think of any occasion when a majority leader within his own party has insisted they (the Senate) proceed on something, there hasn't been a way to work that out," he added.
Biden said he believed the treaty would get at least the two-thirds majority vote needed for approval, even if Lott voted against. Lott has said he has not decided how to vote.
Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle told reporters earlier: "I think that there are enough votes ... to procedurally as well as substantively deal successfully with this treaty."

Lott told reporters he expected the Senate to start debating the chemical weapons issue next week, beginning with consideration of a separate bill proposed by Republican Sen. Jon Kyl of Arizona under which the United States would act unilaterally to deal with the threat, rather than as part of the international treaty.
Treaty supporters opposed the bill which outlaws chemical and biological weapons within the United States and requires U.S. sanctions against other countries using such weapons.
The 4-year-old Chemical Weapons Convention, signed by 161 countries and ratified by 70, bans the development, production, stockpiling, transfer and use of chemical weapons.
Lott said the treaty debate would probably last four or five days, with part of it closed to the press and public while members consider secret material.
Before the treaty can be considered, unanimous agreement must be reached on the terms of the debate and amendments.

Biden and Helms have held a series of meetings to try to work out conditions to the ratification that would satisfy some of Helms's concerns. Beden said agreement had been reached on 21 of 30 issues. In other areas where agreement cannot be reached, the Senate will have to decide.

Helms still strongly opposed the treaty and said he wanted the Foreign Relations Committee to hear testimony from chemical firms that he said opposed the treaty, even though it was strongly backed by the American Chemical Association, the principal industry group.
